goals: Describe how cathode rays and anode rays are produced and list their properties
Compare the charge and mass of the electron, proton and neutron and recall how each was discovered

slides.heading: Subatomic particles and early atomic models
slides.body_md: Part 1: how the electron, proton and neutron were found, and how the first models of the atom were tested.

visual.alt: Table of symbol, charge and mass of the electron, proton and neutron

slides.narration: Welcome. All the matter around you is built from just three kinds of particles: electrons, protons and neutrons. In this part we see how experiments with glowing gas tubes revealed them, how to count them in any atom or ion, and how an experiment with gold foil overturned the first picture of the atom.

slides.heading: The discharge tube
slides.body_md: A glass tube at **very low pressure** carries a **high voltage** between two electrodes. **Cathode rays** leave the cathode; with a perforated cathode, **anode rays** pass through the holes behind it.

visual.caption: Schematic; very low pressure and a high voltage are used.

slides.narration: Look at the two tubes. The gas inside is at very low pressure and a high voltage joins the electrodes. In the top tube, rays stream out of the cathode and make the screen glow, and a metal cross in their path casts a sharp shadow. In the lower tube the cathode has holes, and a different beam of positive particles passes through them.

slides.heading: Properties of cathode rays
slides.body_md: Cathode rays are streams of **electrons**. They are the same whatever the gas or the cathode metal, so the electron is a **universal constituent of matter**. Thomson measured the ratio $e/m_\text{e} = 1.76 \times 10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$.

rows: Rays travel in straight lines from the cathode
Bend towards a positive plate; bend in a magnetic field
Same e/m for every gas and metal
Electrons are present in all atoms
Produce X-rays on striking a heavy metal
Fast electrons give out X-rays on stopping

visual.alt: Table of observations on cathode rays and what each shows

slides.narration: Cathode rays move in straight lines, which is why objects cast sharp shadows. They bend towards a positive plate, so they carry negative charge. They can turn a tiny paddle wheel, so they have mass. Most important, the ratio of charge to mass is the same for every gas and every cathode metal. That means every atom contains these electrons.

slides.heading: Anode rays
slides.body_md: Fast electrons knock electrons out of gas atoms. The **positive ions** formed move towards the cathode, and those passing through its holes form **anode rays** (canal rays). Their $e/m$ depends on the gas; hydrogen gives the largest value because **H⁺ is the lightest**, and it is the **proton**.

visual.alt: Table comparing cathode rays and anode rays

slides.narration: Anode rays are made differently. Electrons in the tube knock electrons out of gas atoms and leave positive ions behind. Those ions drift towards the cathode, and some pass through its holes. Because the particles are ions of the gas, their charge to mass ratio changes with the gas. Hydrogen gives the largest value, and its ion is the proton.

slides.heading: Chadwick and the neutron
slides.body_md: In 1932 Chadwick bombarded **beryllium** with alpha particles. The radiation was **not deflected** by electric or magnetic fields and knocked protons out of paraffin wax, so it was made of **neutral particles of mass close to the proton**.

visual.alt: Nuclear equation: beryllium-9 and an alpha particle form carbon-12 and a neutron
visual.caption: Mass numbers 9 + 4 = 12 + 1; atomic numbers 4 + 2 = 6 + 0.

slides.narration: Chadwick fired alpha particles at beryllium and found a very penetrating radiation. Electric and magnetic fields could not bend it, so it was uncharged. It knocked protons out of paraffin wax with large energy, which needs particles about as heavy as a proton. He had found the neutron. In the equation, mass numbers and atomic numbers balance on both sides.

slides.heading: Worked example: mass of the electron
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The particles of cathode rays have $e/m = 1.76 \times 10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$ and charge $1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$. (a) Find the mass of one particle. (b) How many such particles weigh as much as one proton, mass $1.673 \times 10^{-27}$ kg?

**(a)** $m = \dfrac{e}{e/m} = \dfrac{1.602 \times 10^{-19}}{1.76 \times 10^{11}} = 9.10 \times 10^{-31}$ kg.

**(b)** $\dfrac{1.673 \times 10^{-27}}{9.10 \times 10^{-31}} = 1838$, so about 1840 electrons.

rows: Electron mass is negligible compared with a nucleon

visual.alt: Table of results of the electron mass example

slides.narration: Divide the charge by the charge to mass ratio and you get the mass of the particle, about nine times ten to the power of minus thirty-one kilograms. Dividing the proton mass by this value shows that a proton weighs about eighteen hundred and forty electrons. So almost all the mass of an atom comes from protons and neutrons.

slides.heading: Quick check: the neutron
slides.body_md: Decide what a radiation that no field can bend must be made of.
slides.narration: Quick check. Read the question carefully before choosing. The radiation passed through electric and magnetic fields without bending, which tells you about its charge. It also knocked protons out of paraffin wax, which tells you about its mass. Combine the two clues and pick the particle that fits both.

slides.heading: Atomic number and mass number
slides.body_md: The **atomic number** $Z$ is the number of protons; it fixes the element. The **mass number** $A$ is protons plus neutrons. In the symbol $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$: neutrons $= A - Z$. A neutral atom has $Z$ electrons; a cation has fewer, an anion has more.

visual.alt: Table of counts of particles in an aluminium atom, an aluminium ion and an oxide ion

slides.narration: The atomic number tells you the number of protons and so fixes which element you have. The mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons, so neutrons are the mass number minus the atomic number. An atom has as many electrons as protons. When it becomes an ion, only the electrons change, never the protons or neutrons.

slides.heading: Isotopes and isobars
slides.body_md: **Isotopes**: same $Z$, different $A$ (different neutrons); they behave alike chemically because they have the same electrons. **Isobars**: same $A$, different $Z$; they are different elements.

visual.alt: Table of isotope and isobar pairs

slides.narration: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons. Chlorine thirty-five and chlorine thirty-seven are an example, and the three forms of hydrogen are another. Their chemistry is the same because the electrons are the same. Isobars are different elements that happen to have the same mass number, such as carbon fourteen and nitrogen fourteen.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting particles in ions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in $^{59}_{27}\text{Co}^{3+}$, $^{127}_{53}\text{I}^{-}$ and $^{27}_{13}\text{Al}^{3+}$.

**Co³⁺:** protons 27; neutrons $59 - 27 = 32$; electrons $27 - 3 = 24$.

**I⁻:** protons 53; neutrons $127 - 53 = 74$; electrons $53 + 1 = 54$.

**Al³⁺:** protons 13; neutrons $27 - 13 = 14$; electrons $13 - 3 = 10$.

visual.alt: Table of protons, neutrons and electrons in three ions

slides.narration: For each ion, read the protons from the atomic number, subtract that from the mass number for the neutrons, and then adjust the electrons for the charge. A positive charge means electrons were lost, so there are fewer. A negative charge means electrons were gained, so there are more. Always check that protons minus electrons equals the charge.

slides.heading: Quick check: ions
slides.body_md: Count protons, neutrons and electrons in an ion.
slides.narration: Quick check. Work in three steps. The atomic number gives the number of protons. The mass number minus the atomic number gives the neutrons. Then compare the charge on the ion with the number of protons to find how many electrons it has gained or lost. Check your three numbers against the options.

slides.heading: Thomson’s model
slides.body_md: Thomson (1904) imagined a **sphere of positive charge** with electrons **embedded** in it like seeds in a watermelon. The positive and negative charges cancel, so the atom is neutral. The charge is spread everywhere, so no part of the atom is very dense.

slides.narration: The first model of the atom was proposed by Thomson. Picture a sphere of positive charge with electrons scattered through it like seeds in a watermelon. The total positive charge equals the total negative charge, so the atom is neutral. On the right is the model that replaced it, in which the positive charge sits in a tiny nucleus.

slides.heading: Rutherford’s alpha-scattering experiment
slides.body_md: Alpha particles ($\ce{He^2+}$) were fired at a **very thin gold foil**; flashes on a zinc sulfide screen showed their paths. The computed paths show **bigger deflection for a closer approach** to the positive nucleus.

visual.alt: Alpha-particle scattering: apparatus with a thin gold foil and a zinc sulfide screen, and computed paths of alpha particles passing a nucleus at different distances
visual.caption: Part (b) is not to scale; paths follow repulsion by the nucleus.

slides.narration: In the experiment, alpha particles from a source pass through slits and hit a very thin gold foil. A circular screen coated with zinc sulfide flashes where they land. On the right you can see what happens near one nucleus. Particles far from it hardly bend, those closer bend more, and one aimed almost head on is turned back.

slides.heading: Observations and conclusions
slides.body_md: Rutherford (1911) concluded that the atom has a **small, dense, positively charged nucleus** with electrons outside. The nucleus has a radius of about $10^{-15}$ m against about $10^{-10}$ m for the atom, so the atom is **mostly empty space**.

rows: Most alpha particles pass straight through
Most of the atom is empty space
A few are deflected through small angles
The centre is positively charged and repels alpha particles
Charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus

visual.alt: Table of observations of the scattering experiment and the conclusions

slides.narration: Each observation gives a conclusion. Most particles went straight through, so most of the atom is empty space. A few bent slightly, so the centre is positive and repels them. Very few bounced back, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny nucleus, about one hundred thousand times smaller across than the atom.

slides.heading: Limitations of the nuclear model
slides.body_md: An electron circling the nucleus is **accelerated**, so classical theory says it should **radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus**. The model cannot explain the **stability** of the atom or the **line spectra** of atoms, and says nothing about the arrangement of electrons.

nodes.label: Electron loses energy and spirals in
Atom would collapse; spectrum would be continuous

visual.alt: Flow chart: an orbiting electron radiates energy, spirals inwards and the atom would collapse

slides.narration: Here is the weakness of the nuclear model. An electron moving in a circle is constantly accelerating, and an accelerated charge should give out radiation. It would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, and the atom would collapse in a fraction of a second. Real atoms are stable and give line spectra, so a better model was needed.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the experiment
slides.body_md: Link the rebound of a few alpha particles to the structure of the atom.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask yourself what kind of centre could turn back a fast, heavy, positive alpha particle. Then think about the tiny fraction of particles that were reversed, and what that fraction says about the size of that centre compared with the whole atom. Choose the option that matches both ideas.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Cathode rays: electrons, same e/m for every gas. Anode rays: positive ions of the gas; H⁺ is the proton. Chadwick found the neutron (1932).
Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons; neutrons = A − Z.
Isotopes: same Z, different A. Isobars: same A, different Z.
Thomson: positive sphere with embedded electrons. Rutherford: small, dense, positive nucleus; atom mostly empty space.
Rutherford’s model cannot explain the stability of the atom or line spectra.

visual.alt: Summary table of the three subatomic particles

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Cathode rays are electrons and anode rays are positive ions. Chadwick discovered the neutron. The atomic number counts protons and the mass number counts protons plus neutrons. Thomson placed electrons inside a positive sphere, and Rutherford replaced this with a tiny nucleus. His model could not explain why atoms are stable.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: For ions, change only the electrons: protons and neutrons stay the same.
Write each observation of the foil experiment with its own conclusion.
Give the limitation of Rutherford’s model as stability plus line spectra.
For anode rays, remember that e/m depends on the gas; for cathode rays it does not.
Write nuclear equations with equal mass numbers and equal atomic numbers on both sides.

rows: Changing neutrons when an ion forms
Isotopes share Z; isobars share A

visual.alt: Table of common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips. When an ion forms, only the electrons change. Do not mix up isotopes and isobars: isotopes share the atomic number, isobars share the mass number. When asked about the foil experiment, pair each observation with its conclusion. And remember that anode rays change with the gas, while cathode rays do not.

goals: Explain why wave theory failed for black-body radiation and the photoelectric effect

Use the threshold frequency and KE = h(ν − ν₀) to solve photoelectric problems

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. For a long time light was treated as a wave, described by its wavelength and frequency. But two experiments, the glow of hot bodies and the release of electrons by light, could not be explained that way. The explanation came from the idea that radiant energy comes in small packets called quanta.

slides.heading: What the wave theory could not explain
slides.body_md: Wave theory explains interference, diffraction and $c = \nu\lambda$, with $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. It **fails** for (i) the distribution of energy in the radiation from a **black body** and (ii) the **photoelectric effect**.

rows: Colour of a heated body (black body)
No: predicts unlimited intensity at short wavelengths
No: predicts no threshold and a time lag

visual.alt: Table of phenomena the wave theory explains and those it cannot

slides.narration: The wave theory of light works well for interference, diffraction, reflection and refraction. Wavelength and frequency are linked by the speed of light. But it fails in two places. It cannot explain how a heated body shares its energy among wavelengths, and it cannot explain what happens when light falls on a metal and releases electrons.

slides.heading: Black-body radiation
slides.body_md: A **black body** absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits a spectrum that depends only on temperature. As $T$ rises, the **peak moves to shorter wavelength**, and the total energy rises. Wave theory predicted an intensity that **rises without limit** at short wavelengths.

visual.alt: Intensity of black-body radiation against wavelength at three temperatures, with the wave-theory curve rising without limit at short wavelengths
visual.caption: Peaks move to shorter wavelength as temperature rises.

slides.narration: Here are the measured curves for three temperatures. Each rises to a peak and falls again at short wavelengths. As the temperature goes up the peak moves to shorter wavelength, which is why a hot rod goes from red to white. The dashed line is what wave theory predicted, and it does not match the experiment at all.

slides.heading: Planck’s quantum theory
slides.body_md: Planck (1900): a body emits or absorbs energy **only in discrete packets, quanta**; the energy of one quantum is proportional to the frequency. $$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}, \qquad h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$$ The total energy is a whole-number multiple of $h\nu$, so it is **quantised**.

visual.alt: Table of the quantities in Planck’s equation

slides.narration: Planck proposed that energy is not given out smoothly. A body emits or absorbs it in packets called quanta, and the energy of one quantum is Planck’s constant times the frequency. Since frequency is the speed of light divided by wavelength, short wavelength means large quanta. With this idea the black body curves were explained exactly.

slides.heading: Energy of photons of different colours
slides.body_md: Because $E = hc/\lambda$, **shorter wavelength means more energy per photon**: violet photons carry more energy than red, and ultraviolet more than visible. Radio photons carry very little energy.

visual.alt: Table of photon energies for red, yellow, green, violet and ultraviolet light

slides.narration: The table shows photon energies worked out from the wavelength. Red photons carry the least energy of these and ultraviolet photons the most. This is why ultraviolet light can damage skin and start chemical changes that visible light cannot. The energy of a photon depends only on its frequency, never on how bright the light is.

slides.heading: Worked example: frequency and energy of a photon
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A red laser pointer emits light of wavelength $650\ \text{nm}$. Find the frequency and the energy of one photon. ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

$\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.50 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.62 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

$E = h\nu = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 4.62 \times 10^{14} = 3.06 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

visual.alt: Table of the results for the red laser pointer

slides.narration: First convert the wavelength to metres. Divide the speed of light by it to get the frequency, about four point six times ten to the fourteen hertz. Multiply the frequency by Planck’s constant to get the energy of one photon, about three times ten to the minus nineteen joule. A single photon carries a tiny amount of energy.

slides.heading: Quick check: one photon
slides.body_md: Convert the wavelength to metres and use $E = hc/\lambda$.
slides.narration: Quick check. Convert the wavelength from nanometres to metres before you start. Then multiply Planck’s constant by the speed of light and divide by the wavelength. Remember that energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so a yellow photon should carry a little less energy than a green one. Give your answer in the units asked.

slides.heading: Worked example: number of photons
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 40 W filament bulb turns 5% of its power into visible light of wavelength $550\ \text{nm}$. How many photons does it emit each second?

Light power $= 0.05 \times 40 = 2.0$ W $= 2.0$ J s⁻¹.

$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{5.50 \times 10^{-7}} = 3.61 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

Photons per second $= \dfrac{2.0}{3.61 \times 10^{-19}} = 5.53 \times 10^{18}$.

visual.alt: Table of the quantities in the photon-number example

slides.narration: Only a small part of the bulb’s power leaves as visible light, here two watts. Divide that power by the energy of one photon to count how many photons leave every second. The answer is about five and a half billion billion. So many photons arrive that light seems smooth, even though it is made of separate packets.

slides.heading: The photoelectric effect
slides.body_md: When light of **high enough frequency** falls on a metal surface, **electrons are emitted**. Each electron takes its energy from **one photon**.

nodes.label: Light of frequency ν falls on a metal plate
One photon gives its energy hν to one electron
If hν exceeds the work function, the electron leaves
Extra energy appears as kinetic energy

visual.alt: Flow chart of the photoelectric effect: a photon gives its energy to one electron, which leaves if the energy exceeds the work function

slides.narration: Here is the photoelectric effect in steps. Light of a certain frequency falls on a metal plate. One photon passes all its energy to one electron. If that energy is larger than the energy that binds the electron to the metal, the electron escapes. Whatever energy is left over becomes the kinetic energy of the escaping electron.

visual.alt: Table of observations of the photoelectric effect with the photon explanation

slides.narration: Einstein explained everything by treating light as photons. Below the threshold frequency no single photon can free an electron, however many arrive. Above it, the kinetic energy is the photon energy minus the work function, so it depends on frequency only. Brighter light brings more photons, so more electrons, and each acts at once.

Both lines have the same slope, which is Planck’s constant, and they differ only in where they start. The metal with the lower threshold needs less energetic photons.

slides.heading: Worked example: threshold wavelength and kinetic energy
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The threshold wavelength of a cathode is $560\ \text{nm}$ (given). Find the work function and the maximum kinetic energy of electrons when light of wavelength $420\ \text{nm}$ falls on it.

$W_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{5.60 \times 10^{-7}} = 3.55 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

$E = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{4.20 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.73 \times 10^{-19}$ J, so $\text{KE} = 4.73 \times 10^{-19} - 3.55 \times 10^{-19} = 1.18 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

visual.alt: Table of the work function, photon energy and kinetic energy in the example

slides.narration: Find the work function from the threshold wavelength, using Planck’s constant times the speed of light divided by the wavelength. Then find the energy of the incident photon in the same way. The kinetic energy of the fastest electron is the photon energy minus the work function. Here the photon is the more energetic, so electrons come out.

slides.heading: Quick check: threshold wavelength
slides.body_md: Compare each wavelength with the threshold wavelength.
slides.narration: Quick check. Compare each wavelength with the threshold wavelength, one at a time. Emission happens only when the light has a wavelength shorter than the threshold, which is the same as a frequency higher than the threshold frequency. Decide for each light whether its photons carry enough energy, then pick the option that matches.

slides.heading: Brightness or frequency?
slides.body_md: Frequency decides **whether** electrons are emitted and **how much kinetic energy** they have. Brightness (intensity) decides only **how many** are emitted each second, provided $\nu > \nu_0$.

rows: Twice as many electrons; same KE

visual.alt: Table of the effects of changing frequency and brightness

slides.narration: Remember the roles. Frequency decides whether electrons come out at all and how much energy they carry. Brightness decides only how many come out each second, and only when the frequency is above the threshold. Making dim red light brighter will never release electrons from a metal that needs ultraviolet.

slides.heading: Quick check: brightness
slides.body_md: Decide what doubling the brightness changes.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what brightness really changes. A brighter beam delivers more photons every second, but each photon still has the same energy, because that depends only on frequency. Now decide how the number of electrons leaving the zinc plate each second, and their energy, would be affected by doubling the brightness.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Wave theory failed for black-body radiation and for the photoelectric effect.
Planck: energy is emitted or absorbed in quanta, E = hν = hc/λ, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Photon energy rises as wavelength falls; photons per second = power ÷ energy of one photon.
Photoelectric effect: threshold frequency ν₀; KE = h(ν − ν₀); brightness changes only the number of electrons.

visual.alt: Summary table of the main formulae of Part 2

slides.narration: Summing up Part 2. Wave theory could not explain black body radiation or the photoelectric effect. Planck’s idea that energy comes in quanta equal to Planck’s constant times frequency solved both. Photon energy rises as wavelength falls. In the photoelectric effect, frequency above the threshold decides emission and kinetic energy, and brightness decides only the number of electrons.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Convert nm to metres (× 10⁻⁹) and MHz to hertz (× 10⁶) before substituting.
In a photoelectric problem, first compare the frequency or wavelength with the threshold.
For photons per second, divide the power in watts by the energy of one photon in joules.
For energy per mole of photons, multiply by 6.022 × 10²³ and convert joules to kilojoules.
Say clearly that brightness changes the number of electrons and frequency changes their kinetic energy.

rows: Using nm directly in c = νλ
Saying brighter light gives faster electrons
Using the wavelength where frequency is needed

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Convert units before substituting. In a photoelectric question, compare with the threshold first, because if the frequency is too low the answer is simply no emission. For photons per second, divide power by the energy of one photon. And say clearly that brightness changes the number of electrons while frequency changes their energy.

sections.heading: 1. Cathode rays and anode rays
sections.body_md:
In a discharge tube at very low pressure (about 0.01 mm of mercury) with a high voltage of several kilovolts, **cathode rays** stream from the cathode. They travel in straight lines, cast sharp shadows, make a zinc sulfide screen glow, turn a light paddle wheel, are deflected by electric and magnetic fields as negative particles, give X-rays on hitting a heavy metal, and have the **same e/m** for every gas and cathode: they are **electrons** ($e/m_\text{e} = 1.76 \times 10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$).

With a **perforated cathode**, fast electrons knock electrons out of gas atoms; the **positive ions** drift to the cathode and some pass through the holes as **anode (canal) rays**. They bend the opposite way to cathode rays and their e/m **depends on the gas**: hydrogen gives the largest e/m, because H⁺ (the **proton**) is the lightest.

key_terms.definition_md: Streams of electrons from the cathode of a discharge tube at low pressure.
Streams of positive ions of the gas passing through a perforated cathode; also called canal rays.
The charge of a particle divided by its mass, e/m; the same for all electrons.

sections.heading: 2. The neutron and the three particles
sections.body_md:
Chadwick (1932) bombarded beryllium with alpha particles. The penetrating radiation was **unaffected by electric and magnetic fields** and knocked protons out of paraffin wax: it consisted of **neutrons**, neutral particles of about the proton's mass. The change is $^{9}_{4}\text{Be} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{12}_{6}\text{C} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$.

The electron was found by Thomson, its charge measured by Millikan (oil drops), the proton came from Goldstein's canal rays and Rutherford's work, and the neutron from Chadwick. Almost all the mass of an atom is in the protons and neutrons: a proton weighs about 1837 electrons.

sections.heading: 3. Atomic number, mass number, isotopes and isobars
sections.body_md:
**Atomic number** $Z$ = number of protons (fixes the element); **mass number** $A$ = protons + neutrons; neutrons $= A - Z$. A neutral atom has $Z$ electrons. A cation has $Z$ minus its charge in electrons, an anion has $Z$ plus its charge.

**Isotopes** have the same $Z$ and different $A$; they have the same electron arrangement and so the same chemical behaviour (¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl; ¹²C, ¹⁴C). **Isobars** have the same $A$ and different $Z$ (¹⁴C and ¹⁴N; ²⁴Na and ²⁴Mg).

The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

sections.heading: 4. Thomson’s model, Rutherford’s experiment and nuclear model
sections.body_md:
**Thomson (1904):** a sphere of uniformly spread positive charge with electrons embedded in it (plum-pudding or watermelon model); neutral overall.

**Rutherford (1911):** alpha particles ($\ce{He^2+}$) on a very thin gold foil; a zinc sulfide screen recorded the flashes. **Most passed straight through** (mostly empty space), **a few were deflected** (positive centre repels them) and **very few (about 1 in 20 000) rebounded** (charge and mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus). Nuclear radius about $10^{-15}$ m, atomic radius about $10^{-10}$ m. Electrons move outside the nucleus.

**Limitations:** an accelerating electron should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom would be unstable; the model gives no explanation of line spectra or of how the electrons are arranged.

key_terms.definition_md: The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
A helium nucleus, He²⁺, emitted by some radioactive substances.

sections.heading: 5. Black-body radiation and Planck’s quantum theory
sections.body_md:
A **black body** absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits radiation whose distribution over wavelength depends only on its temperature. As the temperature rises, the **peak moves to shorter wavelength** (red to orange to white). Wave theory predicted intensity rising without limit at short wavelengths, which is wrong.

**Planck (1900):** energy is emitted or absorbed in **quanta**; one quantum has energy $E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$. Photon energy rises with frequency. Number of photons per second $=$ power $\div$ energy of one photon. Energy of one mole of photons $= E N_\text{A}$.

The smallest packet of energy that can be emitted or absorbed, $E = h\nu$.
The constant $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$ linking the energy of a quantum to its frequency.

sections.heading: 6. The photoelectric effect
sections.body_md:
When light of frequency above a **threshold frequency** $
u_0$ falls on a metal, electrons are emitted **instantly**; below $
u_0$ none is emitted however bright the light. The kinetic energy of the electrons depends on the **frequency** only, while the **number** of electrons is proportional to the **brightness**.

Einstein: one photon gives all its energy to one electron, $h
u = W_0 + 	ext{KE}$, with **work function** $W_0 = h
u_0$. A plot of KE against $
u$ is a straight line of slope $h$. The effect shows the **particle nature of light**.

key_terms.definition_md: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal, $W_0 = h\nu_0$.
The lowest frequency of light that can eject electrons from a given metal.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Changing the number of neutrons when an ion forms; only the electrons change.
- Mixing up isotopes (same atomic number) and isobars (same mass number).
- Giving an observation of the foil experiment without its conclusion.
- Writing only "unstable" as the limitation of Rutherford's model without saying why (an accelerating electron radiates energy).
- Using wavelengths in nm or frequencies in MHz without converting to SI units.
- Saying that brighter light gives photoelectrons of greater energy.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Properties of cathode rays and anode rays: one mark for each correct property, with the evidence.
- Counting particles in ions: one mark for each species.
- Photon numericals: formula, substitution in SI units, answer with units.
- Photoelectric numericals: compare with threshold, find the photon energy, then the difference.

cards.front_md: Under what conditions are cathode rays produced?
cards.back_md: In a discharge tube at very low pressure with a high voltage across the electrodes.

cards.front_md: What evidence shows cathode rays are negatively charged?
cards.back_md: They bend towards the positive plate in an electric field.

cards.front_md: Why do cathode rays prove that electrons are in every atom?
cards.back_md: Their e/m is the same for every gas and every cathode metal.

cards.front_md: What does a paddle wheel turned by cathode rays show?
cards.back_md: The rays are particles with mass and momentum.

cards.front_md: Value of e/m for the electron?
How are anode rays produced?
cards.back_md: Electrons ionise the gas; positive ions pass through the holes of a perforated cathode.

cards.front_md: Which gas gives anode rays of the largest e/m?
cards.back_md: Hydrogen: H⁺, the proton, is the lightest positive ion.

cards.front_md: Anode rays versus cathode rays in an electric field?
cards.back_md: They bend the opposite way: anode rays are positive.

cards.front_md: Who discovered the neutron, and how?
cards.back_md: Chadwick (1932), by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.

cards.front_md: Why did Chadwick decide the radiation was neutral?
cards.back_md: Electric and magnetic fields could not deflect it.

cards.front_md: Mass of a proton compared with an electron?
cards.back_md: About 1837 times as great.

cards.front_md: Atomic number: definition?
cards.back_md: Number of protons in the nucleus; it decides the element.

cards.front_md: Mass number: definition?
cards.back_md: Number of protons plus neutrons.

cards.front_md: Number of neutrons in an atom?
cards.back_md: A − Z (mass number minus atomic number).

cards.front_md: Electrons in the ion Al³⁺ (Z = 13)?
cards.back_md: 10: three fewer than the 13 of the atom.

cards.front_md: Isotopes: definition and an example?
cards.back_md: Same atomic number, different mass number; ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.

cards.front_md: Isobars: definition and an example?
cards.back_md: Same mass number, different atomic number; ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N.

cards.front_md: Why do isotopes have the same chemistry?
cards.back_md: They have the same number of electrons.

cards.front_md: The three isotopes of hydrogen?
cards.back_md: Protium (0 neutrons), deuterium (1), tritium (2).

cards.front_md: Thomson’s model in one line?
cards.back_md: A positive sphere with electrons embedded like seeds in a watermelon.

cards.front_md: What did most alpha particles do in the foil experiment?
cards.back_md: Passed straight through: the atom is mostly empty space.

cards.front_md: What did the rebound of a few alpha particles show?
cards.back_md: A tiny, dense, positive nucleus holds the charge and nearly all the mass.

cards.front_md: Size of the nucleus compared with the atom?
cards.back_md: About $10^{-15}$ m against $10^{-10}$ m: 100 000 times smaller.

cards.front_md: Main limitation of Rutherford’s model?
cards.back_md: An accelerated electron should radiate and spiral into the nucleus; no stability.

cards.front_md: What is a black body?
cards.back_md: A body that absorbs all radiation falling on it; its emission depends only on temperature.

cards.front_md: How does the black-body peak change on heating?
cards.back_md: It moves to shorter wavelength.

cards.front_md: Planck’s quantum theory?
cards.back_md: Energy is emitted or absorbed in quanta of energy E = hν.

cards.front_md: Photon energy from wavelength?
cards.back_md: $E = hc/\lambda$, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$ and $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: Photons emitted per second?
cards.back_md: Power in watts divided by the energy of one photon in joules.

cards.front_md: Einstein’s equation for photoelectrons?
cards.back_md: KE = hν − hν₀ = h(ν − ν₀).

cards.front_md: What do brightness and frequency each control?
cards.back_md: Brightness: number of electrons. Frequency: whether they come out and their KE.

cards.front_md: What is the work function?
cards.back_md: Minimum energy to remove an electron from the metal surface, W₀ = hν₀.

questions.stem_md: A narrow beam leaves the cathode of a low-pressure discharge tube and passes between two charged metal plates, the upper plate being positive. The beam bends:

options.text_md: downwards, towards the negative plate, showing that it carries positive charge
neither way, since the beam is electrically neutral
upwards, towards the positive plate, showing that it carries negative charge
sideways, out of the plane of the plates, whatever their charge

questions.solution_md: Like charges repel and unlike attract, so a beam bending towards the positive plate is negative — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Cathode rays were studied in tubes filled in turn with hydrogen, air and neon, using cathodes of iron, copper and aluminium. The charge-to-mass ratio of the particles in the rays was found to be:

options.text_md: largest for hydrogen and smallest for neon
the same in every case, so the particles are a common constituent of all matter
largest for the lightest cathode metal
different for every pair of gas and metal

questions.solution_md: e/m was identical whatever the gas or the cathode, so the particles (electrons) are present in all atoms — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Anode rays are obtained from tubes containing hydrogen, helium and argon in turn. Which gas gives positive particles with the largest charge-to-mass ratio?

options.text_md: argon, because its atoms are the largest
helium, because it is an inert gas
hydrogen, because its positive ion is the lightest
all three, because the ratio is the same for any gas

questions.solution_md: The particles are positive ions of the gas. Charge is similar (one unit) but mass is least for H⁺, so e/m is greatest for hydrogen — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In 1932 a penetrating radiation from beryllium bombarded with alpha particles was seen to knock fast protons out of paraffin wax and to pass undeviated through electric and magnetic fields. The radiation consisted of:

options.text_md: electrons released from the beryllium atoms
neutral particles with a mass close to that of the proton
positively charged helium nuclei
very short-wavelength radiation with no mass

questions.solution_md: No deflection in fields means no charge; knocking out protons of comparable mass needs particles of about the same mass — neutrons, option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a property of anode rays but NOT of cathode rays?

options.text_md: The charge-to-mass ratio of the particles changes with the gas in the tube
They travel in straight lines in the absence of fields
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields
They make a zinc sulfide screen glow

questions.solution_md: Cathode-ray particles are the same electrons for every gas. Anode-ray particles are positive ions of the gas, so e/m varies with the gas — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Thomson showed that the particles in cathode rays have the same charge-to-mass ratio in every gas. Using $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ and $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$, calculate $e/m_\text{e}$ in units of $10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$.
Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding a thin sheet of ___ with alpha particles.
questions.solution_md: The target was beryllium: alpha particles on beryllium release neutrons.

questions.stem_md: Match each experimenter with the finding for which he is credited.

options.text_md: Chadwick
Thomson
Goldstein
Millikan

match_right.text_md: positive (canal) rays in a perforated-cathode tube
the charge on the electron, from oil drops

questions.solution_md: Chadwick → neutron (q); Thomson → electron (s); Goldstein → canal rays (p); Millikan → electron charge from oil drops (r).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In an electric field, anode rays bend in the direction opposite to cathode rays.

**Reason (R):** Anode rays carry positive charge, whereas cathode rays carry negative charge.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both true; opposite charges bend in opposite directions, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When cathode rays strike a heavy metal anode, X-rays are produced.

**Reason (R):** Cathode rays are deflected by a magnetic field.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but deflection in a magnetic field does not account for X-ray emission (caused by sudden stopping of the fast electrons) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Write four properties of cathode rays observed in a gas discharge tube at low pressure.

answer.model_answer_md: Cathode rays (i) travel in straight lines away from the cathode and cast sharp shadows of objects in their path; (ii) are deflected by electric and magnetic fields in the sense expected for negative charge; (iii) make a fluorescent screen glow and can turn a light paddle wheel, so they are streams of particles with mass and energy; (iv) have the same e/m whatever the gas or the cathode material.

questions.solution_md: Four properties, half a mark each.

questions.stem_md: In a discharge tube with a perforated cathode, how are anode rays produced? Why does the charge-to-mass ratio of their particles depend on the gas filling the tube?

answer.model_answer_md: Fast cathode-ray electrons knock electrons out of the gas atoms, leaving positive ions. These ions move towards the cathode and those that pass through its holes form a beam behind it, the anode (canal) rays. The particles are ions of the gas itself, so their mass, and hence e/m, depends on which gas is used; hydrogen gives the largest e/m because H⁺ is the lightest.

questions.solution_md: Ionisation of gas by electrons; ions mass depends on gas.

marking_scheme.step: Production of positive ions and rays through the holes
e/m depends on the mass of the ion of the gas

questions.stem_md: Compare the electron, the proton and the neutron by writing, in a table, the symbol, the approximate charge in coulomb and the approximate mass in kilogram of each, and name its discoverer.

answer.model_answer_md: Electron: symbol $\ce{e-}$, charge $-1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C, mass $9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, discovered by J. J. Thomson (cathode rays). Proton: symbol $\ce{p+}$ (or $^1_1\text{H}^{+}$), charge $+1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C, mass $1.673 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, from Goldstein's canal rays and Rutherford's work. Neutron: symbol n, charge 0, mass $1.675 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, discovered by Chadwick in 1932.

questions.solution_md: Electron, proton and neutron data.

questions.stem_md: Describe Chadwick's experiment in which beryllium is bombarded with alpha particles. Write the balanced nuclear equation for the change in beryllium-9 and state how Chadwick showed that the radiation was neither charged nor gamma rays.

answer.model_answer_md: Alpha particles from a polonium source struck a beryllium target, which gave out a highly penetrating radiation. The change is $^{9}_{4}\text{Be} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{12}_{6}\text{C} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$ (mass numbers 9 + 4 = 12 + 1; atomic numbers 4 + 2 = 6 + 0). The radiation was not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, so it was uncharged, and it knocked protons out of paraffin wax with energies too large for gamma rays, so it had to consist of particles of nearly the proton's mass: neutrons.

questions.solution_md: Experiment; equation; evidence for neutral particles.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the conditions under which cathode rays are produced in a discharge tube. [2]

(b) State the observation that shows the particles of cathode rays are negatively charged. [1]

(c) The charge-to-mass ratio of the particles is $1.76 \times 10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$ and their charge is $1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$. Calculate the mass of one particle. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A glass tube fitted with two metal electrodes is pumped down to a very low pressure (about 0.01 mm of mercury) and a high voltage of several thousand volts is applied across the electrodes. Rays then stream from the cathode towards the anode and make the glass or a screen at the far end glow.

(b) The rays bend towards the positive plate in an electric field, and bend in the sense expected for negative charge in a magnetic field.

(c) $m = \dfrac{e}{e/m} = \dfrac{1.602 \times 10^{-19}}{1.76 \times 10^{11}} = 9.10 \times 10^{-31}$ kg.

questions.solution_md: Low pressure and high voltage; deflection towards positive plate; m = 9.10 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

marking_scheme.step: (a) High voltage and rays from the cathode

questions.stem_md: A galvanised nail loses zinc ions into water. The number of protons, neutrons and electrons in one $^{64}_{30}\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ion is, respectively:
questions.solution_md: Protons = Z = 30; neutrons = 64 − 30 = 34; electrons = 30 − 2 = 28 for a 2+ ion — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A chemist isolates an ion of mass number 37 that contains 20 neutrons and 18 electrons. The ion is:
questions.solution_md: Protons = 37 − 20 = 17, so the element is chlorine; 18 electrons give a charge of 17 − 18 = −1, so $^{37}\text{Cl}^{-}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of species consists of isotopes of the same element?
questions.solution_md: Isotopes have the same atomic number (6 for both carbon species) but different mass numbers — option (a). The pairs (b) and (c) are isobars.

questions.stem_md: Species X (atomic number 18, with 22 neutrons) and species Y are isobars of each other. If Y has atomic number 20, the number of neutrons in Y is:
questions.solution_md: Mass number of X = 18 + 22 = 40. Isobars share the mass number, so Y has 40 − 20 = 20 neutrons — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A nuclear reactor uses heavy water, $\ce{D2O}$, in which D is deuterium $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ and oxygen is $^{16}_{8}\text{O}$. One molecule of this heavy water contains how many neutrons?
questions.solution_md: Each D has 2 − 1 = 1 neutron, so two D give 2; $^{16}$O has 16 − 8 = 8; total 2 + 8 = 10 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A sealed capsule for dating studies holds $1.40\ \text{g}$ of the isotope carbon-14, of molar mass $14\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the total number of neutrons in the capsule, in units of $10^{23}$. ($N_\text{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: Moles of atoms $= \dfrac{1.40}{14} = 0.100$ mol, so atoms $= 0.100 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{22}$. Neutrons per atom $= 14 - 6 = 8$, so neutrons $= 8 \times 6.022 \times 10^{22} = 4.82 \times 10^{23}$; in units of $10^{23}$: $4.82 \times 10^{23} / 10^{23} = 4.82$.

questions.stem_md: Atoms of different elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called ___.
questions.solution_md: Same mass number, different atomic number: isobars.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 behave almost identically in chemical reactions because their atoms contain the same number of electrons.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Chemical behaviour is decided by the electron arrangement, which depends on the number of protons (and so electrons), not on the number of neutrons.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Protium, deuterium and tritium differ in their mass numbers.

**Reason (R):** The three isotopes of hydrogen contain different numbers of protons in their nuclei.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true (1, 2 and 3), but R is false: all three have one proton and differ in neutrons (0, 1, 2) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two isobars always contain the same number of neutrons.

**Reason (R):** Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same atomic number.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Isobars share the mass number and have different atomic numbers, so their neutron numbers differ. Both statements are false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A laboratory bottle contains bromide ions $^{79}_{35}\text{Br}^{-}$ and another holds iron(III) ions $^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}^{3+}$. Find the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in each ion.

answer.model_answer_md: $\text{Br}^{-}$: protons 35; neutrons $79 - 35 = 44$; electrons $35 + 1 = 36$. $\text{Fe}^{3+}$: protons 26; neutrons $56 - 26 = 30$; electrons $26 - 3 = 23$.

questions.stem_md: Define isotopes and isobars. Give one example of each from the species ¹²C, ¹⁴C, ¹⁴N and ³⁵Cl.

answer.model_answer_md: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons), e.g. ¹²C and ¹⁴C. Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers, e.g. ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N.

questions.solution_md: Definitions with an example each.

questions.stem_md: Name the three isotopes of hydrogen and, for the neutral atom of each, give the mass number and the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons.

answer.model_answer_md: Protium (¹H): mass number 1, 1 proton, 0 neutrons, 1 electron. Deuterium (²H or D): mass number 2, 1 proton, 1 neutron, 1 electron. Tritium (³H or T): mass number 3, 1 proton, 2 neutrons, 1 electron. They share the atomic number 1 and so behave alike chemically.

questions.solution_md: Protium, deuterium, tritium with counts.

questions.stem_md: A species contains 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons. Identify the element, write the symbol of the species with its mass number, atomic number and charge, and say whether it is a cation or an anion.

answer.model_answer_md: Z = 16, so the element is sulfur. Mass number $= 16 + 16 = 32$. Charge $= 16 - 18 = -2$. The species is $^{32}_{16}\text{S}^{2-}$, the sulfide ion, an anion because it has gained two electrons.

questions.solution_md: Sulfur; mass number 32; charge −2; anion.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define atomic number and mass number, and state which of the two decides the identity of an element. [2]

(b) Find the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in each of the following: $^{31}_{15}\text{P}^{3-}$, $^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $^{19}_{9}\text{F}^{-}$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus; the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons. The atomic number decides the identity of the element.

(b) $\text{P}^{3-}$: 15 protons, $31 - 15 = 16$ neutrons, $15 + 3 = 18$ electrons. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$: 12 protons, $24 - 12 = 12$ neutrons, $12 - 2 = 10$ electrons. $\text{F}^{-}$: 9 protons, $19 - 9 = 10$ neutrons, $9 + 1 = 10$ electrons.

questions.stem_md: In the model of the atom proposed by J. J. Thomson, the positive charge is:

options.text_md: concentrated at the centre, with electrons far outside
carried by neutral particles sitting in the nucleus
confined to the surface of the atom like a shell
spread evenly through the whole atom, with the electrons embedded in it

questions.solution_md: Thomson pictured a uniformly positive sphere with embedded electrons (plum-pudding model) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A newspaper article says that in the gold-foil experiment about one alpha particle in 20 000 bounced almost straight back. This tiny fraction suggests that:

options.text_md: the positive charge and nearly all the mass are packed into a very small nucleus
gold atoms contain no electrons at all
the positive charge is spread evenly over the whole atom
electrons repel alpha particles very strongly

questions.solution_md: Only a head-on approach to a tiny, dense, positive centre can reverse an alpha particle, so such events are rare — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An atom has a radius of about $10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ and its nucleus a radius of about $10^{-15}\ \text{m}$. If the atom were scaled up to a stadium of radius $100\ \text{m}$, the nucleus would be about the size of:

options.text_md: a small coin, about 1 cm
a football, about 10 cm
a bus, about 10 m
a grain of sand, about 1 mm

questions.solution_md: Ratio of radii $= 10^{-10}/10^{-15} = 10^{5}$, so the nucleus would have radius $100 / 10^{5} = 0.001$ m $= 1$ mm — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The particles fired at the gold foil in Rutherford’s experiment were alpha particles. An alpha particle is the same as:

options.text_md: a helium nucleus, He²⁺
a hydrogen nucleus, H⁺
an electron ejected from a nucleus
a neutral helium atom

questions.solution_md: An alpha particle has two protons and two neutrons, a helium nucleus with charge +2 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In Rutherford’s model an electron revolves in a circular path round the nucleus. According to classical electromagnetic theory such an electron would:

options.text_md: stay in its path for ever without radiating
jump to a higher orbit by absorbing light
radiate energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus
be pushed out of the atom by the nucleus

questions.solution_md: An accelerated charge radiates, so the electron would lose energy and fall into the nucleus — the instability of the model, option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the scattering experiment on a thin gold foil, the few alpha particles that were deflected through large angles were those that:

options.text_md: collided with the electrons of a gold atom
were absorbed by the gold atoms and re-emitted
passed very close to a nucleus and were strongly repelled by it
passed through the empty space between atoms

questions.solution_md: Strong deflection needs a strong repulsion, which occurs only on a close approach to the small positive nucleus — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the gold-foil experiment, an alpha particle that rebounds has been repelled by the positively charged nucleus of a gold atom.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Alpha particles and the nucleus are both positive; a close, nearly head-on approach reverses the alpha particle.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Almost all alpha particles pass straight through a thin gold foil.

**Reason (R):** An alpha particle is a helium nucleus carrying a charge of +2.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the identity and charge of the alpha particle do not explain why it passes straight through; the reason is that most of the atom is empty space, with the mass and positive charge concentrated in a tiny nucleus — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A Rutherford atom with an electron circling the nucleus would be unstable.

**Reason (R):** A charged particle that is accelerated emits electromagnetic radiation and loses energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Circular motion is accelerated motion, so the electron radiates and spirals inwards; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each model or experiment with its main idea.

options.text_md: Thomson’s model
Gold-foil experiment
Rutherford’s model
Alpha particle

match_right.text_md: cannot explain why atoms are stable
evidence for a small, dense nucleus
electrons embedded in a positive sphere

questions.solution_md: Thomson’s model → s; gold-foil experiment → q; Rutherford’s model → p; alpha particle → r.

questions.stem_md: State two observations of the alpha-particle scattering experiment on gold foil and the conclusion drawn from each.

answer.model_answer_md: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil: most of the atom is empty space. A very few were turned back through large angles (about one in twenty thousand): the positive charge and the mass are concentrated in a very small, dense nucleus. (A small number were deflected slightly: the nucleus is positive and repels the alpha particles.)

questions.solution_md: Two observations with conclusions.

questions.stem_md: Describe the model of the atom given by Thomson. How does it account for the atom being electrically neutral?

answer.model_answer_md: Thomson proposed that an atom is a sphere of uniformly distributed positive charge in which the negatively charged electrons are embedded, like seeds in a watermelon. The positive charge on the sphere is exactly equal in magnitude to the total negative charge of the electrons, so the atom is neutral overall.

questions.solution_md: Sphere with embedded electrons; charges balance.

questions.stem_md: Give three limitations of Rutherford’s nuclear model of the atom.

answer.model_answer_md: First, it cannot explain the stability of the atom: an electron moving round the nucleus is accelerated and should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus. Second, it predicts a continuous spectrum as the electron spirals in, whereas atoms emit line spectra of definite wavelengths. Third, it says nothing about how the electrons are arranged or how much energy they have.

questions.solution_md: Instability, line spectra, arrangement of electrons.

questions.stem_md: In a gold-foil experiment about $1$ alpha particle in $20\,000$ is turned back through more than $90^\circ$. Calculate how many particles are expected to turn back when $5.0 \times 10^{5}$ alpha particles strike the foil, and explain what this small fraction tells us about the size of the nucleus.

answer.model_answer_md: Number turned back $= \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{5}}{20\,000} = 25$. Only a head-on approach to a nucleus can reverse an alpha particle, so such events are rare. Because only about one particle in twenty thousand meets a nucleus closely, the nucleus must occupy a minute fraction of the atom's volume (its radius is about $10^{-15}$ m against $10^{-10}$ m for the atom).

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{5}}{20\,000} = 25$ particles; the nucleus is very small.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the alpha-particle scattering experiment of Rutherford. [1]

(b) State the three observations made and the conclusion drawn from each. [3]

(c) State one limitation of the nuclear model. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A narrow beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source was directed at a very thin gold foil surrounded by a zinc sulfide screen, and the flashes on the screen showed where the particles went.

(b) Most particles passed straight through: most of the atom is empty space. A few were deflected through small angles: the centre of the atom is positively charged and repels them. Very few (about one in twenty thousand) rebounded: the positive charge and nearly all the mass lie in a very small, dense nucleus.

(c) An electron circling the nucleus would radiate energy and spiral in, so the model cannot explain the stability of the atom (or line spectra).

questions.solution_md: Experiment; three observations and conclusions; limitation.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write two differences between Thomson's model and Rutherford's model of the atom. [2]

(b) Explain why the result of the scattering experiment could not be explained by Thomson's model, and state how Rutherford's model accounts for it. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In Thomson's model the positive charge and mass are spread through the whole atom; in Rutherford's they are concentrated in a tiny nucleus. In Thomson's model the electrons are embedded in the sphere; in Rutherford's they move outside the nucleus.

(b) In Thomson's atom the positive charge is spread out, so no part of it can exert a strong enough force to turn an alpha particle back; at most small deflections would occur. The rebound of a few particles requires a concentrated repulsive centre. Rutherford's nucleus provides this, and because it is so small most alpha particles pass through the empty space around it without any deflection.

questions.solution_md: Two differences; failure of Thomson and success of Rutherford.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Spread-out charge cannot cause large deflection

questions.stem_md: A blacksmith heats an iron rod. It first glows dull red, then orange, and finally white-hot as its temperature rises. This happens because, on heating:

options.text_md: the rod starts to emit light for the first time
the wavelength at which most energy is emitted shifts towards shorter wavelengths
only red light is ever emitted by iron
the rod emits equal energy at every wavelength

questions.solution_md: The peak of the black-body emission curve moves to shorter wavelengths as temperature rises, so the colour moves from red towards white — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A radio station at 91.1 MHz, a green LED at 530 nm, a hospital ultraviolet lamp at 254 nm and a dental X-ray set at 0.05 nm are compared. Photons of the highest energy come from:

options.text_md: the radio station
the green LED
the dental X-ray set
the ultraviolet lamp

questions.solution_md: E = hc/λ, so the shortest wavelength (0.05 nm, the X-ray) gives the largest photon energy — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Blue light falls on a metal plate in a photocell but no electrons are emitted. Which change will certainly cause photoelectrons to be emitted?

options.text_md: making the blue light much brighter
shining the blue light for a longer time
using a larger plate of the same metal
using ultraviolet light, which has a higher frequency

questions.solution_md: Emission needs photons with frequency above the threshold; brightness, time and plate size do not change photon energy — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A photocell has a metal whose threshold wavelength is 500 nm. Light of 400 nm and light of 600 nm are tried in turn. Photoelectrons are emitted by:

options.text_md: the 600 nm light only
the 400 nm light only
both lights
neither light

questions.solution_md: Emission needs λ shorter than the threshold wavelength (higher frequency than threshold): 400 nm < 500 nm, whereas 600 nm > 500 nm — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The energy of a photon of wavelength 250 nm is compared with that of a photon of wavelength 750 nm. The first photon has ____ times the energy of the second.

options.text_md: one-third
nine
one-ninth

questions.solution_md: $E \propto 1/\lambda$, so $E_1/E_2 = \lambda_2/\lambda_1 = 750/250 = 3$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two lamps each give out light at a power of 1 W, one at 400 nm and the other at 800 nm. In every second:

options.text_md: both lamps emit the same number of photons
the 400 nm lamp emits twice as many photons as the 800 nm lamp
the 800 nm lamp emits four times as many photons
the 800 nm lamp emits twice as many photons as the 400 nm lamp

questions.solution_md: A photon of 800 nm has half the energy of one of 400 nm, so for equal power twice as many photons are needed — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The work function of a metal in a vacuum photocell is $3.3 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ (given). Its threshold frequency is closest to ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$):
True or false? If the brightness of ultraviolet light falling on a zinc plate is doubled while its frequency stays above the threshold, the number of photoelectrons emitted per second doubles.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Twice as many photons arrive each second and each can free one electron, so the number of electrons doubles (their energy is unchanged).

questions.stem_md: According to Planck, radiant energy is emitted or absorbed by a body in tiny packets, each called a ___.
questions.solution_md: The packet of energy is a quantum (E = hν).

questions.stem_md: A sodium vapour street lamp gives yellow light of wavelength $589\ \text{nm}$. Calculate the energy of one photon of this light, in units of $10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)

A torch LED gives out light of wavelength $480\ \text{nm}$ at a power of $2.0\ \text{W}$. Calculate the number of photons it emits each second, in units of $10^{18}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)

An ultraviolet lamp used to sterilise laboratory benches emits radiation of wavelength $254\ \text{nm}$. Calculate the energy of one mole of its photons, in kJ. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $N_\text{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

A photocell has a cathode of threshold frequency $5.4 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$ (given). Light of frequency $8.2 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$ falls on it. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in units of $10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)
What is a black body? State two ideas of Planck’s quantum theory that were used to explain the radiation from a heated black body.

answer.model_answer_md: A black body is an ideal object that absorbs all radiation falling on it and, when heated, emits radiation of all wavelengths whose distribution depends only on its temperature. Planck proposed that energy is emitted or absorbed only in discrete packets (quanta), and that the energy of one quantum is proportional to the frequency of the radiation, E = hν.

questions.solution_md: Definition; quantisation and E = hν.

questions.stem_md: Ultraviolet light from a small lamp releases electrons from a zinc plate, but an intense red lamp does not. Explain this using the idea of threshold frequency.

answer.model_answer_md: Each electron absorbs one photon at a time. Ultraviolet photons have a frequency above the threshold frequency of zinc, so each carries more than the work function and can eject an electron. Red photons have a frequency below the threshold, so no single photon has enough energy, however many of them arrive.

questions.solution_md: One photon per electron; ultraviolet above threshold, red below.

marking_scheme.step: One photon ejects one electron if hν exceeds the work function
UV above and red below threshold

questions.stem_md: A microwave oven in a canteen works at a frequency of $2450\ \text{MHz}$. Calculate the wavelength of its radiation and the energy of one photon. ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)
State three observations of the photoelectric effect that cannot be explained by the wave theory of light, and state how the photon picture explains them.

answer.model_answer_md: First, no electrons are emitted below a threshold frequency, however intense the light; wave theory expects enough energy to build up from any light, but a photon below the threshold has too little energy to free an electron. Second, the kinetic energy of the electrons depends on the frequency, not the brightness; each electron takes the energy of one photon, hν, minus the work function. Third, emission is instantaneous even for dim light, because one photon gives its energy to one electron at once.

questions.solution_md: Threshold, KE depends on frequency, no time lag.

questions.stem_md: The threshold wavelength of the cathode of a photocell is $620\ \text{nm}$ (given). Calculate (a) the work function in joules and (b) the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted when light of wavelength $400\ \text{nm}$ falls on it. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$)

A radio transmitter radiates a power of $50\ \text{kW}$ at a frequency of $99.5\ \text{MHz}$. Calculate the energy of one photon and the number of photons emitted per second, and say why radio waves do not seem to arrive in separate packets. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

answer.model_answer_md: $E = h\nu = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 9.95 \times 10^{7} = 6.59 \times 10^{-26}$ J. Number per second $= \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{4}}{6.59 \times 10^{-26}} = 7.58 \times 10^{29}$. Each photon carries an almost immeasurably small energy and so many arrive every second that the radiation behaves as a smooth, continuous wave.

questions.solution_md: $E = 6.59 \times 10^{-26}$ J; $N = 7.58 \times 10^{29}$ photons per second.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain what is meant by black-body radiation and why the wave theory failed to account for the intensity of radiation at short wavelengths. [2]

(b) State Planck's quantum theory and write the equation for the energy of a quantum. [1]

(c) Calculate the energy of one photon of ultraviolet light of wavelength $300\ \text{nm}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$) [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A black body absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits a spectrum that depends only on its temperature. Wave theory predicted that the intensity would rise without limit towards short wavelengths (the "ultraviolet catastrophe"), but measured curves rise to a peak and fall again.

(b) Planck: a body emits or absorbs energy only in discrete packets called quanta; the energy of one quantum is proportional to the frequency, $E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$.

(c) $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{3.00 \times 10^{-7}} = 6.63 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

questions.solution_md: Black body and failure of wave theory; E = hν; $E = 6.63 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
